Skeptical evidence review, round 2
29 September 2026. Internal second-round review after reading the shared synthesis and both protocol
and economic first-round reports. This review reuses earlier bridge research. The checks are independent
recalculations of shared saved records, not independent data-provider corroboration or external
assurance. No transactions, privileged calls or state-changing simulations were performed. Origin/
Morpho-specific analysis was not reopened.
Status: complete for the identified historical main-paper revision. The reviewed revision is identified by
its SHA-256 in the round-2 evidence batch.
Challenge to the skeptical objections
The clarified H1 is correct: an authorized source receipt can finance a local purchase if the exact
claim is accepted and the output is funded. Independent intrinsic value or demonstrated source
solvency is not universally required for a finite contract execution. A configured AMM can transfer
existing PLS for a claim without inspecting remote collateral. A funded lender can lend against a price its
rules accept even if later liquidation cannot recover that value. The first transaction may succeed while a
loss remains with the pool, lender or other claim holder.
The round-1 reference to economically usable backing must therefore not be read as an additional
universal EVM precondition. Actual output assets and applicable contract predicates are the relevant
execution conditions. Source custody, realizable backing and redemption matter when the claim being
tested is that the system is backed, solvent, repeatable or able to support future prices. They are
separate propositions from the successful transfer of a finite funded amount.
The economic review already makes this distinction in its funded-lender counterexample. Its opening
phrase “valuable source claim” is unnecessarily restrictive unless “valuable” means only that an
executable bid is available. The protocol review's no-bid counterexample defeats the unconditional
inference from nominal units to purchasing power; it does not defeat a stipulated funded AMM exchange.
This is a wording correction and a boundary on the objections, not new evidence that such a configured
funding path currently exists.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 366

Likewise, absence of an observed end-to-end transaction is not proof that no route could execute. It is
appropriate evidence against the proposition that this paper has established that complete deployed
route. A route can be proved executable by other sufficiently complete state and implementation
evidence; an actual historical witness is one strong method, not the only conceivable method. The
current record still leaves essential configuration and source links unresolved.
Views retained from round 1
The GRT and ARB destination mint observations remain strong and token-specific. They show that
pre-existing L1 token escrow is not always necessary for delivery through an authorized integration.
They do not independently prove source custody, burns, investment or redemption.
The raw ARB source-block and timestamp words remain implausible chronology. No amount of
additional destination supply arithmetic converts those words into an independently verified source
deposit.
The selected router/gateway census remains bounded. Current default routes, historical routes and
token issuer permissions are different facts. A source-backed new representation need not be the
exact token already accepted by a destination pool or issuer.
Specific governance events prove particular protocol actions. Queuing, execution, proxy authority,
module authority and human control remain distinct. Historical association does not establish a
coordinated stabilization plan.
The 66 manifest checks, raw event recount, supply recalculation and numerical checks strengthen
internal reproducibility. They do not make the common RPC independently authenticated, remove
the disclosed pre-fork query gap, or establish source-chain history.
An externally referenced finite PLS execution value is a valid stipulated target. It is not automatically
executable external-dollar liquidation of all received PLS, and a successful one-time sale is not a
durable peg.
Effect of the clarified proposition
H1 is deliberately existential and conditional. Its high support must be read with its conditions attached.
A bridge can change the location and ownership of an exclusive claim, while a destination pool or lender
supplies the spendable assets. This is a useful accounting result. It is not evidence that administrative
control creates that funding or makes an arbitrary stablecoin a permitted issuer input.
The objective is not to demand solvency for every possible transaction. It is to avoid switching
conclusions midway through the argument: an executable exchange proves an exchange; a backed
representation requires source backing evidence; a self-financing cycle requires its liabilities and losses
to reconcile; sustained support requires a specified horizon and funded response to the relevant flows.
Reproducibility and remaining disagreement
The review package should preserve the original and revised papers with hashes, identify the H1
wording change, publish the final proposition definitions beside any scores, and make the ignored raw
evidence bundle available if external reproduction is intended. The shared records make the reviews
correlated. Linear averaging summarizes their judgments; it is not new on-chain evidence or statistical
verification of the thesis.
This review agrees with the other reviews' main distinction between conditional coherence and
demonstrated deployment. This review rejects any stronger skeptical statement that a funded
mechanical swap necessarily fails merely because the input's backing is economically weak. Conversely,
This review does not regard such a swap's success as evidence that the backing is strong.

Inspection of the revised paper
The revision materially improves the claim boundary. The abstract now separates historical mechanisms,
a stipulated financing ledger and a finite market theorem. It explicitly declines to infer funding from
validator control or nominal copied balances and leaves the complete pinned deployment unestablished.
The main text now distinguishes custody, solvency, redemption liquidity and purchasing capacity; adds
the independent DAI/USDT supply-cap constraints; accounts for pending bridge rights and return; and
specifies route-level rejection conditions.
The new ledger supplies the missing accounting connection without pretending it is an observed quote.
Its investor commits 1,000 source shares, receives and sells 1,000 representations, then spends the
counterparty's existing PLS. The counterparty loses exactly the buyer's PLS budget and gains the
represented claim. Source custody retains 1,000 shares; the source vault's underlying and share
obligations remain unchanged. The pDAI market gains the spent PLS and loses the pDAI acquired by the
investor. No independent copy of the source underlying appears in this accounting.
This review checked the numerical connection against the existing independently recomputed finite-sale
example: approximately 2,167,281,613.012984 PLS input acquires 684,271.838699 pDAI and leaves
approximately 315,728.161301 pDAI in the modeled pool. Initial pDAI inventory equals final pool
inventory plus the investor's purchase. The stipulated counterparty funds the sequence before the
purchase; there is no negative intermediate PLS balance in the described order. The existing fee-free and
separately funded transaction-cost qualifications remain necessary. The ledger is a conditional
composition witness, not bytecode verification of an exact deployed composition.
The asynchronous identity is now expressly a simple lossless model and counts pending rights once.
That repairs the overbroad implication that destination supply always equals committed escrow at every
intermediate moment. Actual message finality, cancellation and release behavior still require the exact
bridge implementation if a deployed claim is made.
The revised falsifier table appropriately tests a complete custody/redemption model. Its source-right and
return requirements should not be reinterpreted as universal preconditions for a single local AMM trade.
A local trade may execute before the economic weakness of a source claim is known; failure of
redemption then defeats the backed/repeatable interpretation, not the fact that the trade occurred. The
paper's explicit acceptance-versus-solvency distinction supports this reading.
Governance can change some roadblocks: evidence versus assumption
It is conceivable that careful operators with the necessary effective authority and an executable
governance process could mitigate some identified limitations. A zero cap is a present parameter, not a
theorem that every future configuration must retain it. Available inventory can change. Compatible
integrations can be introduced where the actual control and interfaces permit them. Those statements
do not prove that the named wallets possess all required authority, that every proposal can execute, or
that changing a setting supplies new economic resources.

These are classifications of possible authorized state differences, not a sequence for changing
governance. A successful governance vote is only one part of an effective process: timelock/executor
authority, the target's actual permissions and application validation determine the resulting capabilities.
Observed execution proves its particular path and date; historical proposal participation does not prove
the ability to amend every later target.
The final main-paper governance section correctly adds an issuer qualification: authorized control of the
exact issuer can create additional token balances. That is different from changing a lender's oracle or
borrowing limit, and does not itself guarantee an executable PLS bid. Native PLS issuance would require
a separate consensus-level assumption, not ordinary application governance.
No accounting conservation requirement disappears through governance. An implementation change
can change claims, issue authorized token units or redistribute existing assets, but this is a changed
mechanism whose effects must be described, not evidence that the previous route already worked.
Likewise, current insufficient cash is not permanent impossibility, while a claim to pay existing assets
without any funded source remains incomplete under the stated accounting.

Final epistemic judgments
These central scores and ranges express subjective support for the exact propositions. They are neither
calibrated event probabilities nor forecasts. Low H2/H4 scores concern what the current paper
establishes; they do not estimate the probability of future governance changes or future price
movements. H1 now means accepted and funded, without an intrinsic-value requirement. H6 is an
existential claim about some roadblocks, not a universal guarantee.

The small ranges around near-logical propositions represent interpretive and review uncertainty, not
frequencies. The governance clarification raises no conflict with low H2: a potentially changeable
configuration can still be unestablished or unavailable at the specific audited snapshot. the round-2
assessment supports the revised conditional result while retaining all source provenance, exact-identity,
funding, attribution and reproducibility limitations.
